papers.title: Beyond Point Photo-$z$ Estimates: Normalizing Flows for Tomographic $N(z)$ Reconstruction with DESI DR1
papers.authors: Zhuo Chen, Antoine Rocher, Kwan Chuen Chan, Jean-Paul Kneib
papers.abstract: Accurate calibration of tomographic redshift distributions, $N(z)$ is essential for cosmological analysis of weak lensing data. We investigate conditional normalizing flows (NFs) and compare their performance with random forest (RF) and quantile random forest (QRF) models. We consider DESI galaxy and quasar targets from DESI DR1 spectroscopic data and with the photometry from Legacy Surveys DR10. We train on 1.1 million sources and test on 2.0 million sources in a non-overlapping sky region ($0<z_{\rm spec}<4.5$). For point estimation, the NF achieves the lowest scatter and outlier fraction at $0<z_{\rm spec}<1.6$ and outperforms both baselines across all three metrics at $z_{\rm spec}>1.6$. By introducing distribution-level metrics like Wasserstein distance and JS divergence, we find that stacking NF posterior PDFs provides more accurate tomographic $N(z)$ reconstruction than QRF, particularly at high redshifts. For $z_{\rm median}>2.5$, the NF achieves a smaller absolute mean-redshift bias ($0.060\pm0.031$ versus $0.318$) and higher probability overlap ($0.905\pm0.008$ versus $0.787$) than QRF. We apply redshift-dependent post-hoc PDF calibration derived from a held-out validation sample. After calibration, the absolute mean-redshift biases in four bins spanning $0.2<z_{\rm median}<1.0$ range from $0.0016$ to $0.0019$, with central values below referring benchmark $0.002(1+z)$. In the highest-redshift bin, calibration further reduces the bias to $0.016\pm0.011$. Our results demonstrate the potential of NF PDFs for tomographic $N(z)$ reconstruction while highlighting challenges in transferring models across galaxy populations.

conclusions: For single-object point estimates at low redshift ($0 < z_{\rm spec} < 1.6$), the Normalizing Flow achieves the lowest normalized scatter ($\sigma_{\rm NMAD} = 0.0223 \pm 0.0002$) and catastrophic outlier rate ($3.79\%$), while at high redshift ($z_{\rm spec} > 1.6$) it beats both tree-based baselines across all metrics ($\sigma_{\rm NMAD} = 0.1015$, outlier fraction $25.74\%$).

When stacking individual PDFs to reconstruct tomographic redshift bins, the NF reproduces the true spectroscopic distribution shapes, widths, and extended tails better than QRF, especially in the sparse highest-redshift bin ($z_{\rm median} > 2.5$) where it slashes the absolute mean-redshift bias from $0.318$ (QRF) down to $0.060 \pm 0.031$ and raises distribution overlap from $0.787$ to $0.905$.

Applying a post-hoc empirical cumulative distribution function (CDF) calibration from a validation sample brings the NF mean-redshift bias across four intermediate bins ($0.2 < z_{\rm median} < 1.0$) down to $0.0016\text{--}0.0019$, meeting the stringent Stage IV Euclid accuracy requirement of $|\Delta z| \lesssim 0.002(1+z)$ on this spectroscopic target sample.

The authors caution that while NFs excel at capturing complex redshift uncertainties, run-to-run variance across random seeds and selection biases when transferring models trained on bright spectroscopic targets to deeper, broader photometric survey populations remain key hurdles.
ai.relevance_reason: Provides background on photometric redshift $N(z)$ calibration and Euclid weak lensing accuracy benchmarks, though it focuses on observational machine learning pipelines rather than theoretical beyond-$\Lambda$CDM modelling or simulations.
ai.summary: In wide-field imaging surveys like Euclid and LSST, cosmological analyses of weak lensing and galaxy clustering rely on grouping hundreds of millions of galaxies into broad redshift slices ("tomographic bins") using broadband colours (photometric redshifts, or photo-$z$'s). Because colour-redshift degeneracies often make an individual galaxy's redshift probability density function (PDF) asymmetric or multi-peaked, simply assigning a single best-guess redshift per galaxy biases the overall redshift distribution $N(z)$ of each bin. The authors apply conditional Normalizing Flows (NFs)—generative neural networks that smoothly deform a simple Gaussian into complex, multi-modal probability distributions via invertible transformations—to estimate full photo-$z$ PDFs for over 3 million galaxies and quasars cross-matched between DESI DR1 spectroscopy and Legacy Surveys DR10 photometry. By stacking these continuous NF posteriors and applying a post-hoc statistical recalibration, they reconstruct tomographic $N(z)$ profiles across independent sky patches significantly more accurately than standard tree-based machine learning baselines (Random Forests and Quantile Random Forests).

papers.title: A multiprobe $Λ$CDM consistency analysis with gravitational-wave standard sirens
papers.authors: T. M. C. Abbott, M. Aguena, F. Andrade-Oliveira, S. Avila, D. Bacon, D. Brooks, H. Camacho, R. Camilleri, G. Campailla, A. Carnero Rosell, J. Carretero, R. Cawthon, C. Chang, L. N. da Costa, M. E. da Silva Pereira, S. Desai, H. T. Diehl, P. Doel, A. Ferté, D. L. Hollowood, K. Honscheid, D. Huterer, D. Laghi, S. Lee, S. MacBride, J. L. Marshall, I. McMahon, J. Mena-Fernández, R. Miquel, J. Muir, J. Myles, R. L. C. Ogando, A. A. Plazas Malagón, J. Prat, M. Rodríguez-Monroy, R. Rosenfeld, S. Samuroff, E. Sanchez, D. Sanchez-Cid, I. Sevilla-Noarbe, M. Soares-Santos, E. Suchyta, M. E. C. Swanson, V. Vikram, N. Weaverdyck, J. Weller, M. Yamamoto (DES Collaboration)
papers.abstract: Multi-messenger cosmology offers an independent path to stress-test the $\Lambda$CDM model as gravitational wave (GW) catalogs grow in size. We present the first multiprobe assessment of $\Lambda$CDM tensions incorporating GW standard sirens: LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Collaboration (LVK) fifth Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog (GWTC-5.0) standard sirens are combined with Dark Energy Survey (DES) Year 6 weak lensing and galaxy clustering (3$\times$2pt), baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO), and type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia), together with Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) BAO, and confronted with primary cosmic microwave background (CMB) measurements from Planck, the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT), and the South Pole Telescope (SPT). All probes are analyzed under homogeneous priors and combined via normalizing flows, and we quantify the $S_8$ discrepancy and $H_0$ tension with respect to CMB. Adding standard sirens to the 3$\times$2pt analysis improves the constraints in the $\Omega_m$-$S_8$ plane by $\sim$30%, while constraining $H_0$ to 6.2%. We present cosmological constraints from the low-redshift probes including standard sirens, yielding $S_8 = 0.793 \pm 0.010$, $\Omega_m = 0.308^{+0.007}_{-0.006}$, and $H_0 = 69.4^{+4.1}_{-4.4}$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$. At current GW sensitivity, however, both the $S_8$ discrepancy and the $H_0$ tension remain essentially unchanged. Our analysis nonetheless delivers the first assessment of $\Lambda$CDM tensions computed with standard sirens included among the probes, and establishes them as a mature cosmological probe -- ready to be combined on equal footing with established datasets in forthcoming surveys such as the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), Euclid, and Roman.

conclusions: Adding GWTC-5.0 standard sirens to the DES Year 6 $3\times 2\text{pt}$ weak lensing and galaxy clustering analysis improves the figure of merit in the $\Omega_m$–$S_8$ plane by $\sim 30\%$ due to complementary degeneracy directions in $\Omega_m$–$H_0$, while constraining $H_0$ to $6.2\%$ precision.

Combining all low-redshift probes (DES Y6 $3\times 2\text{pt}$, BAO, SNe Ia, DESI DR2 BAO, and GWTC-5.0 sirens) yields $S_8 = 0.793 \pm 0.010$, $\Omega_m = 0.308^{+0.007}_{-0.006}$, and $H_0 = 69.4^{+4.1}_{-4.4}\text{ km s}^{-1}\text{ Mpc}^{-1}$.

When compared against combined primary CMB data (Planck + ACT DR6 + SPT-3G), the 1D $S_8$ discrepancy sits at $2.83\sigma$ for $3\times 2\text{pt}$ alone and $2.6\sigma$ for the full low-$z$ combination, while full parameter-space tensions stay between $2.16\sigma$ and $2.44\sigma$.

At current GWTC-5.0 sensitivity, adding standard sirens shifts tension metrics by $\lesssim 0.1\sigma$ and adds negligible constraining power once BAO and SNe Ia are already included, serving primarily as a proof-of-concept and systematics cross-check ahead of Euclid, LSST, and Roman.

ai.summary: Gravitational-wave "standard sirens"—compact binary mergers whose luminosity distances are calibrated directly by general relativity—offer an independent geometric probe to test the $H_0$ and $S_8$ cosmological tensions without relying on traditional electromagnetic distance ladders. In this paper, the DES Collaboration performs the first multiprobe $\Lambda$CDM consistency check that integrates LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (GWTC-5.0) standard sirens with flagship low-redshift datasets: DES Year 6 weak lensing and galaxy clustering ($3\times 2\text{pt}$), DES and DESI DR2 BAO, and DES Year 5 Type Ia supernovae. They utilize both the single "bright siren" with an electromagnetic counterpart (GW170817) and 235 "spectral sirens," which infer source redshifts statistically by matching detector-frame masses against features in the intrinsic compact-object mass distribution. Using normalizing flows (`tensiometer`) under homogenized priors, the authors combine these low-redshift posteriors and quantify multi-dimensional parameter tensions against combined primary CMB measurements from Planck, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G. This establishes a pipeline for integrating gravitational waves on equal footing with electromagnetic surveys like Euclid and LSST, providing a cross-check with largely uncorrelated systematics.

papers.title: How tightly can PBH abundance information constrain scalar-induced gravitational waves?
papers.authors: Boliang Yu, Ruixin Zhou, Zi-Yu Tang
papers.abstract: Primordial black hole (PBH) abundances and scalar-induced gravitational waves (SIGWs) probe the same primordial fluctuations through different physical weights. We examine the predictive power of precise synthetic information on absolute PBH abundances over a finite stellar-mass interval, together with an exact total abundance and external population bounds. For Gaussian perturbations under a fixed quantum chromodynamics (QCD) formation prescription, two smooth, symmetric lognormal spectra satisfy the same abundance conditions while producing nonproportional leading-order SIGW spectra. The two spectra differ by about 20% when averaged over the lower of two adjacent nanohertz windows but by nearly a factor of 60 in the higher-frequency window, so the difference cannot be represented by a single rescaling of the gravitational-wave background. Peak position and width compensate with amplitude in the abundance calculation, while the higher-frequency window draws almost all its energy from scalar-mode pairs with both wavenumbers above the primordial peak. Under the principal abundance benchmark, local finite-width components yield larger contrasts at a fixed nanohertz frequency through distinct mode couplings under both the QCD and stochastic peak-curvature formation prescriptions. For a separately generated population, extending mass information over most of its abundance restricts the lognormal peak-position and width compensation and reduces the higher-window contrast, while the unequal window responses persist. These results show why joint PBH-SIGW inference must propagate primordial shapes compatible with the PBH abundance information rather than assign one tensor template to a single abundance fit.

conclusions: Two smooth lognormal curvature power spectra with identical PBH abundance properties ($\chi^2_{\mathrm{PBH}} \le 1$ across $[1, 101]\,M_\odot$ and an exact total dark matter fraction $f_{\mathrm{all},0} \simeq 7.25\times 10^{-4}$) produce SIGW spectra that differ by $\sim 20\%$ in a lower nanohertz frequency window ($\overline{F}_1 \simeq 1.2$), but by a factor of $\sim 58$ in the adjacent higher-frequency window ($\overline{F}_2 \simeq 58$).

This degeneracy occurs because peak position, width ($\Delta \simeq 0.42$ vs. $0.82$), and amplitude ($P_* \simeq 0.013$ vs. $0.011$) compensate in the smoothed variance governing PBH formation, whereas more than $98\%$ of the higher-frequency GW window is sourced by pairs of scalar modes with wavenumbers above the primordial peak ($q, p > k_*$).

Allowing a more flexible, multi-component primordial spectrum amplifies the discrepancy: under the same QCD collapse prescription, the GW ratio at the reference frequency $f_1 = 1.98\,\mathrm{nHz}$ jumps from $2.7$ (single lognormal) to $15.5$, and the higher-frequency window ratio reaches $1.1\times 10^3$.

Extending PBH mass measurements to cover the turnover and main body of the mass function restricts the peak-width compensation and reduces the high-frequency GW uncertainty, proving that joint PBH–PTA inference must marginalize over compatible primordial shapes rather than relying on a single tensor template.
ai.summary: In the early Universe, large-amplitude primordial curvature perturbations on small scales can simultaneously collapse into primordial black holes (PBHs) and source a stochastic background of scalar-induced gravitational waves (SIGWs) at second order in perturbation theory. Because both observables stem from the same primordial power spectrum $\mathcal{P}_\zeta(k)$, one might hope that measuring the PBH mass distribution would tightly predict the companion nanohertz SIGW signal probed by pulsar timing arrays (PTAs). The authors test this assumption by constructing synthetic PBH abundance measurements across the stellar-mass window $[1, 101]\,M_\odot$—combining a fixed total PBH dark matter fraction with external astrophysical bounds and thermal softening during the QCD phase transition—and searching for distinct primordial power spectra that yield identical PBH populations. They demonstrate that PBH formation and SIGW generation weight primordial wavenumbers differently: PBH abundance depends exponentially on smoothed variance moments, allowing changes in peak position, width, and height to compensate one another, whereas high-frequency SIGWs are quadratically sourced by specific resonant pairs of small-scale modes above the primordial peak. Consequently, even tightly constrained PBH mass distributions leave massive degeneracies in the shape and amplitude of the high-frequency SIGW spectrum.

papers.title: Cuscuton Fifth Force: Implications of Non-Dynamical Scalars for Structure Growth
papers.authors: Adam Smith, Ilaria Andrei, Maria Mylova, Niayesh Afshordi
papers.abstract: The cuscuton is a scalar field that obeys a constraint rather than an evolution equation, so it modifies gravity without adding a propagating scalar degree of freedom. We study the cosmology of effective cuscuton theory when matter is minimally coupled in the Jordan frame, and therefore conformally coupled to the cuscuton in the Einstein-frame. We derive the background and linear perturbation equations and show that the algebraic cuscuton response mediates a fifth force even though the scalar itself does not propagate. The same conformal factor also changes Einstein-frame particle masses and the friction of matter perturbations, tying the strength and sign of the force to the background evolution rather than to an independent coupling. We study a power-law family of models which contain both tracking solutions and sign-switching solutions; in the latter the effective cuscuton density runs from negative during matter domination to a positive, cosmological-constant-like value today. Using a modified version of CLASS, including the induced particle-mass dependence of recombination, we illustrate the corresponding changes to CMB temperature and linear matter power spectra for benchmark models, without fitting to data. In the strongest benchmarks the fifth force changes the effective gravitational coupling on sub-horizon scales by about one percent, smaller than the accompanying changes to the matter power spectrum and the acoustic scale. For the sign-switching solutions this change is negative over most of cosmic history, so a non-propagating field can weaken rather than strengthen gravitational attraction.

conclusions: Even without a propagating scalar degree of freedom, the algebraic constraint governing the cuscuton mediates a quasi-static fifth force and modifies Hubble friction in the matter growth equation, with its strength and sign fixed directly by the background expansion rather than an independent coupling parameter.

Across both tracking and sign-switching power-law benchmarks, the direct fifth-force correction to the effective gravitational coupling $G_{\rm eff}/G_N$ on sub-horizon scales is at most $\sim 1\%$ (peaking around $10^{-2}$ for tracking parameter $\lambda = -10^2$ and sign-switching parameter $\zeta = 10^{-2}$).

In the sign-switching regime—where the effective cuscuton energy density transitions from negative during matter domination to positive at late times—the fifth-force correction is negative for $a \lesssim 0.8$, acting as a repulsive fifth force that weakens gravitational attraction over most of cosmic history.

Cosmological observables are dominated by the modified background expansion and evolving electron mass during recombination rather than the $1\%$ fifth force itself, shifting CMB acoustic peaks by a few percent and suppressing the linear matter power spectrum by $\sim 25\%$ at $k = 1\,h\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}$.

These cosmological $G_{\rm eff}$ predictions cannot be naively extrapolated to Solar System tests because strong local spatial gradients $|\nabla\phi|$ around localized sources can violate the timelike-gradient condition $X = \dot{\phi}^2 - |\nabla\phi|^2 > 0$, causing the effective cuscuton description to break down in the nonlinear regime.

ai.summary: Scalar-tensor modified gravity models usually introduce an extra propagating scalar wave that mediates a fifth force, which requires screening mechanisms to pass tight Solar System bounds. The "cuscuton" is a special class of scalar field with a degenerate kinetic term whose equation of motion acts purely as an algebraic constraint rather than a dynamical wave equation—meaning it modifies gravity while propagating only the two standard tensor modes of General Relativity. In this paper, the authors formulate an effective cuscuton theory where matter is minimally coupled in the Jordan frame (and thus conformally coupled in the Einstein frame) and implement it into a modified version of `CLASS` and `HyRec` to study structure growth and the CMB in power-law "tracking" and "sign-switching" dark energy regimes. They demonstrate that even without a propagating scalar mode, the field's instantaneous algebraic response to matter density perturbations still mediates a cosmological fifth force, though its effects on the matter power spectrum and CMB are tightly locked to—and overshadowed by—the accompanying background expansion and time-varying electron mass.

papers.title: Bayesian and frequentist constraints on dark energy parameterizations using non-CMB data
papers.authors: Shubham Barua, Ansh Chandrakar, Shantanu Desai
papers.abstract: Data from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) BAO combined with the cosmic microwave background (CMB) have provided evidence for dynamical dark energy (DDE) with a phantom crossing ($w(z) < -1$) when constraining $w_0-w_a$ parameterizations. Given the tension between BAO and CMB data within $\Lambda$CDM, we use only non-CMB data: Type Ia Supernovae (SNe) from the DES-Dovekie compilation, DESI BAO DR2, Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) and Redshift-Space-Distortion (RSD) measurements. We use the dataset combinations GRB$+$BAO, BAO$+$SNe and GRB$+$BAO$+$SNe, each with RSD. We perform both Bayesian and frequentist analyses of two quintessence-inspired thawing dark energy parameterizations: the thawing quintessence parameterization (TQD) and the Algebraic Thawing parameterization (AT), together with the Chevallier-Polarski-Linder (CPL) and the Generalized Emergent Dark Energy parameterizations (GEDE). The GRB sample, used in this work, contributes only marginally to the constraints, while SNe tighten them considerably. The CPL equation of state shows a phantom crossing at $z\sim 0.5$, while TQD and AT improve the best-fit $\chi^2$ over $\Lambda$CDM, without showing phantom crossing. When SNe are included, TQD is preferred by the Bayes factor (moderately), AIC and DIC (positively). For CPL and AT, AIC and DIC prefer the extended model positively, while the Bayes factor weakly prefers $\Lambda$CDM over CPL and is inconclusive for AT. This difference is consistent with the Occam penalty from the prior volume in the Bayes factor. GEDE, with the DE density restricted to be suppressed at high redshifts is disfavored by all three metrics. Hence, the preference for DDE depends on the parameterization, the dataset and the comparison metric used.

conclusions: In the standard CPL ($w_0 w_a$) parameterization using DESI DR2 BAO + SNe + GRBs + RSD, $w_0 = -0.83^{+0.07}_{-0.08}$ ($\sim 2\sigma$ away from $-1$) and $w_a = -0.47^{+0.47}_{-0.58}$ (consistent with $0$ within $1\sigma$), exhibiting a phantom crossing around $z \sim 0.5$ at $2\text{--}3\sigma$ significance.

The two quintessence-inspired thawing parameterizations (TQD and AT) improve the best-fit $\chi^2$ over $\Lambda$CDM without ever crossing into the phantom regime ($w < -1$), showing that non-phantom scalar field dynamics can explain the late-time expansion data well.

Model preference depends heavily on the statistical metric: while AIC and DIC favor CPL, TQD, and AT when supernovae are included, the Bayes factor penalizes the larger prior volume of CPL (weakly preferring $\Lambda$CDM over CPL) and only moderately favors the TQD model.

Matter density ($\Omega_{m0} \approx 0.306$) and structure growth ($\sigma_8 \approx 0.82\text{--}0.83$) remain robust across all dark energy parameterizations and agree well between Bayesian and frequentist methods; high-redshift Gamma-Ray Bursts add negligible constraining power compared to SNe.
ai.relevance_reason: Directly addresses dynamical dark energy ($w_0 w_a$ and quintessence parameterizations) and cosmological constraints from DESI DR2 BAO and supernovae, which are medium-relevance topics in your research profile.
ai.summary: Recent results combining DESI Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO) with the CMB have hinted that dark energy might be evolving over time and even crossing the "phantom divide" ($w(z) < -1$, where dark energy density grows with expansion, violating standard energy conditions). However, because CMB and BAO data already have a mild tension in their preferred matter density $\Omega_{m0}$ within $\Lambda$CDM, it is unclear how much of this dynamical dark energy signal is an artifact of forcing those datasets together. To isolate late-time physics, the authors drop the CMB entirely and test four dynamical dark energy parameterizations—including standard $w_0 w_a$ (CPL), emergent dark energy (GEDE), and two "thawing quintessence" models where a scalar field sits frozen at $w = -1$ early on before rolling at late times—using only DESI DR2 BAO, Type Ia supernovae (DES-Dovekie), Gamma-Ray Bursts, and Redshift-Space Distortions ($f\sigma_8$). By comparing both Bayesian MCMC posteriors and frequentist profile likelihoods (which avoid prior-volume effects), they show that whether dynamical dark energy or phantom crossing is actually preferred depends heavily on the chosen parameterization and statistical penalty metric.

papers.title: foraois: Fast, Flexible Extended Press-Schechter Merger Trees with a General First-Crossing Solver
papers.authors: C. Power (ICRAR-UWA), S. Balu (U Seville)
papers.abstract: We present foraois (Gaelic for Forest; FAW-reesh), an open-source Python framework for generating Monte Carlo dark matter halo merger tree histories. foraois separates the description of the linear density field, the physics of halo collapse, and the algorithmic construction of halo merger histories, allowing different cosmologies, collapse prescriptions, and tree building approaches to be combined within a common framework. The package implements two approaches to the same merger-tree problem of sampling progenitor masses in the excursion-set picture: the semi-empirical algorithm of Parkinson, Cole, & Helly (2008), which applies a fitted correction to the EPS progenitor distribution, and the numerical solution of the Markovian first-crossing equation developed by Zhang & Hui (2006), which for the default real-space top-hat window is an approximation to the correlated-walk problem. Linear matter power spectra for Cold, Warm, and Fuzzy Dark Matter (CDM, WDM, and FDM) can be supplied, while the modular collapse treatment provides an extension point for alternative barrier models. The framework also supports constrained merger histories based on the Brownian-bridge construction of Nadler et al. (2023). We run extensive validation and scaling tests, and also show an illustrative example of coupling foraois to a light-weight semi-analytical model of galaxy formation.

conclusions: The modular architecture of `foraois` cleanly decouples cosmological variance $S(M)$, collapse barriers $B(S,z)$, first-crossing statistics, and discrete tree-sampling algorithms, enabling independent testing of Cold, Warm, and Fuzzy Dark Matter (CDM, WDM, FDM) power spectra and scale-dependent collapse models.

Comparing the empirical Parkinson et al. (2008) branching algorithm against the theoretical Zhang & Hui (2006) first-crossing sampler under identical cosmological inputs reveals a persistent systematic offset in mean surviving progenitor mass even at fine timesteps, demonstrating that differences trace directly to the underlying progenitor transition probabilities rather than numerical time-stepping artifacts.

The framework supports constrained main-branch histories via a Brownian-bridge construction (conditioning haloes to pass through specific progenitor masses at earlier redshifts) and seamlessly couples to semi-analytic galaxy formation models like `Ashvini` to evaluate how alternative dark matter models alter the stellar-to-halo mass relation.

Key physical approximations are kept transparent for testing: the Zhang–Hui solver assumes Markovian random walks even when paired with a default real-space top-hat filter (which induces correlated steps), and moving-barrier merger trees are currently supported only in the serial Zhang–Hui builder.

ai.summary: To model how galaxies form and evolve without running expensive $N$-body simulations for every parameter choice, cosmologists often generate dark matter halo "merger trees" using Extended Press–Schechter (EPS) excursion-set theory—a statistical method where smoothed linear density perturbations perform a random walk as a function of mass scale until they cross a critical collapse threshold (the "barrier"). In beyond-$\Lambda$CDM cosmologies, halo assembly can change both because the linear matter power spectrum $P(k)$ is altered and because the physics of gravitational collapse makes the collapse barrier $B(S,z)$ depend on mass scale (a "moving barrier"). The authors introduce `foraois`, an open-source, modular Python package that explicitly separates the linear power spectrum, the collapse barrier, the mathematical solver for when random walks first cross that barrier, and the Monte Carlo algorithm that samples discrete halo mergers across time. The code implements both the widely used empirical Parkinson et al. (2008) branching prescription and the general numerical first-crossing solver of Zhang & Hui (2006), alongside a "Brownian-bridge" method to generate histories constrained to hit specific progenitor masses at chosen redshifts. This clean separation matters because it allows researchers to isolate how individual physical assumptions—such as switching between Cold, Warm, and Fuzzy Dark Matter or changing the tree-sampling algorithm—propagate into halo assembly histories and downstream semi-analytic galaxy formation models.

papers.title: The nucleon is not a hard sphere: screening fifth forces with Skyrmions
papers.authors: Philippe Brax, Clare Burrage, Adam Moss
papers.abstract: Laboratory searches for chameleon and symmetron fifth forces increasingly rely on individual nucleons as sources or probes, but model them as uniform spheres. Motivated by the Skyrme picture, we instead consider a nucleon profile with a constant-density core and an $r^{-6}$ pion tail, together with its exponential truncation at the physical pion mass. We derive analytic screening charges for the uniform sphere and the $r^{-6}$ profile, and extend the comparison to the exponential truncation at the physical pion mass using numerical solutions. Because the outer tail is too dilute to be screened at any coupling strength, the $r^{-6}$ tail produces a power-law enhancement over the sphere charge in strong screening, and the exponential tail has a weaker, logarithmic enhancement. Propagating this difference through the published analyses, nucleon-sourced exclusion regions extend systematically further into the strongly coupled regime. For example, symmetron constraints from neutron interferometry at $\mu=1\,\mathrm{keV}$ reach maximal self-couplings about $1.4$ orders of magnitude higher than for a uniform-sphere neutron ($3.0$ orders of magnitude in the chiral limit),and at the dark-energy scale the hydrogen $1s$--$2s$ chameleon bound reaches couplings $1.8$ orders of magnitude weaker than for a uniform-sphere proton ($2.4$ in the chiral limit), overtaking the muonium bound.

conclusions: In the strong-screening regime, the chiral-limit $r^{-6}$ Skyrmion tail yields a power-law enhancement of the screening charge relative to a uniform sphere of equal mass and RMS radius ($\mathcal{Q}_{\rm tr}/\mathcal{Q}_{\rm sph} \propto \varepsilon_{\rm tr}^{-1/4}$ for chameleons and $\propto s^{1/2}$ for symmetrons), while the physical pion-mass exponential truncation ($2m_\pi a \approx 0.43\text{--}0.78$) produces a weaker logarithmic enhancement.

Analytic screening charge expressions derived for the $r^{-6}$ profile (using thin-shell matching for chameleons and modified Bessel functions $I_{\pm 1/4}$ in the massless near zone for symmetrons) match full non-linear numerical boundary-value solutions to within $\sim 10^{-6}$.

Re-evaluating laboratory data with the pion-truncated Skyrmion profile pushes exclusion bounds significantly deeper into the strong-coupling regime: neutron interferometry symmetron bounds at $\mu = 1\,\mathrm{keV}$ reach maximal self-couplings $\sim 1.4$ orders of magnitude higher ($3.0$ in the chiral limit) than for a hard-sphere neutron.

For chameleons at the dark-energy scale ($\Lambda = 2.4\,\mathrm{meV}$), the hydrogen $1s\text{--}2s$ spectroscopy bound on the matter coupling reaches values $\sim 1.8$ orders of magnitude stronger ($2.4$ in the chiral limit) than under the uniform-sphere proton assumption, overtaking the competing muonium bound.

ai.summary: Scalar-tensor modified gravity models like chameleons and symmetrons rely on screening mechanisms—where the fifth force is dynamically suppressed in high-density environments—to evade solar-system and laboratory tests. Precision laboratory experiments (such as ultracold neutron bouncing, neutron interferometry, and hydrogen spectroscopy) probe these theories using individual protons and neutrons, which previous analyses simplified as uniform, hard spheres of nuclear density. In this paper, the authors replace the hard-sphere approximation with a more realistic nuclear matter distribution based on the Skyrme model (an effective field theory where baryons emerge as topological solitons called Skyrmions), modeling the nucleon with a constant-density core and an $r^{-6}$ pion tail (both in the massless-pion chiral limit and with a physical Yukawa truncation at the pion mass). Because this diffuse outer tail cannot be fully screened even at very strong matter couplings, a Skyrmion nucleon retains a significantly larger "screening charge" (the unscreened fraction of its mass sourcing the exterior fifth force) than a uniform sphere of identical mass and RMS radius. This theoretical refinement systematically expands existing laboratory exclusion bounds into the strongly coupled regime without requiring any new experimental data.

papers.title: Thirty years of primordial deuterium abundances: A provenance-aware statistical reanalysis
papers.authors: Richard de Grijs, Giuseppe Bono
papers.abstract: (ABRIDGED:) Primordial deuterium provides one of the most precise observational tests of Big Bang nucleosynthesis, yet the published literature is built on a comparatively small number of high-redshift absorption systems. We construct a provenance-aware database of 957 published primordial-D/H values from 247 publications spanning 1994--2026 and trace observational entries, wherever possible, to their underlying physical absorbers. Of the 795 observational entries, 80.1 percent represent reused individual or compilation values; only 11.4 percent correspond to new determinations of individual absorption systems. Although 52 distinct absorbers are identified overall, the eight most frequently represented systems account for 62.0 percent of all identifiable absorber mentions. An inverse Herfindahl--Hirschman measure applied to our full database gives an effective representation equivalent to only 16.28 equally represented absorbers, demonstrating that the published literature is strongly concentrated around a much smaller effective subset. Despite this strong internal dependence, the modern consensus value of $10^5({\rm D/H})\simeq2.5$ is robust to alternative absorber-level treatments and survives removal of the eight dominant systems. However, the apparent precision of literature-level compilations is more sensitive to repeated representation than a simple count of published values implies. We also identify a synchronised transition in the compilation literature around 2013--2014, associated with increasingly selective and homogeneous analyses while older individual values continued to circulate. The modern D/H consensus is therefore robust in central value, but the underlying literature is less statistically independent than its publication density suggests. This thus highlights the importance of provenance-aware analysis in precision cosmology.

conclusions: Of the 795 observational $\mathrm{D/H}$ entries published between 1994 and 2026, $80.1\%$ are reused individual or compilation values, while only $11.4\%$ (91 entries) represent genuinely new measurements of individual absorption systems.

Although 52 distinct physical absorbers appear in the literature, the eight most frequently cited systems account for $62.0\%$ of all mentions; an inverse Herfindahl–Hirschman concentration index yields an effective sample size of just $N_{\rm eff} = 16.28$ equally weighted absorbers.

Despite this heavy concentration, the modern central value of $10^5(\mathrm{D/H}) \simeq 2.5$ is physically robust: taking the median across 15 modern individual-absorber medians gives $2.5000$, and removing the eight dominant systems altogether still yields $10^5(\mathrm{D/H}) = 2.4960 \pm 0.0265$.

A sharp transition toward apparent convergence occurred around 2013–2014 (anchored by homogeneous reanalyses like Cooke et al.'s "Precision Sample"), demonstrating that while the central baryon-density constraint is solid, the effective statistical independence of the literature is much lower than raw publication counts imply.
ai.summary: Primordial deuterium ($\mathrm{D/H}$) is a "baryometer" for Big Bang nucleosynthesis (BBN): because stars only destroy deuterium, measuring its abundance in pristine, high-redshift gas clouds (damped Lyman-$\alpha$ quasar absorption systems) directly pins down the cosmic baryon density $\Omega_b h^2$. While hundreds of primordial $\mathrm{D/H}$ values have been published over the last thirty years with seemingly percent-level concordance, these numbers are not statistically independent because astronomers repeatedly re-observe, re-analyse, and re-compile the same small handful of clean quasar sightlines. The authors construct a "provenance-aware" database of 957 published $\mathrm{D/H}$ values from 247 papers (1994–2026), tracing every number back to its underlying physical gas cloud and separating genuinely new observations from recycled values and compilations. This matters because naive meta-analyses that treat published compilations as independent data points severely overestimate the statistical sample size and risk letting a few over-represented sightlines or homogeneous analysis pipelines dictate precision cosmological priors.

papers.title: Recovering Missing Degrees of Freedom in Simulation-Trained Field-Level Generative Models
papers.authors: Masato Shirasaki, Shiro Ikeda
papers.abstract: Simulation-trained generative models are emerging as a powerful framework for field-level inference in cosmology, particularly in strongly nonlinear regimes where analytical approaches become intractable. However, the finite size of training datasets often leads to variance shrinkage, indicating that part of the realization-level variability of the underlying physical process is not captured by the learned generative dynamics. In this Letter, we interpret variance shrinkage as a diagnostic of missing effective degrees of freedom and introduce physics-informed latent modifications to the generative dynamics of a continuous normalizing flow. We show that these latent corrections recover a substantial fraction of the missing variability without requiring additional training simulations. Using weak-lensing field-level inference as a representative cosmological application, we further demonstrate through posterior analysis that the learned latent directions are actively exploited during inference and behave as effective nuisance parameters that absorb part of the mismatch between the training and target distributions. As a result, the model exhibits improved robustness to out-of-distribution shifts in field-level inference. Our work establishes variance shrinkage as a practical diagnostic for identifying missing degrees of freedom in simulation-trained generative models and provides a framework for recovering them through physics-informed modifications of generative dynamics.

conclusions: A baseline CNF trained on 10,000 gravity-only $\kappa\text{TNG}$ weak-lensing maps accurately matches mean power spectra and peak counts within $0.5\sigma$, but suffers from severe variance shrinkage across realizations.

Introducing a 20-parameter physics-informed correction to the flow velocity field recovers a substantial fraction of the missing realization-level variance without requiring new training simulations, with a single dominant latent mode ($\theta_{\text{add}}$) acting as a scale-dependent growth-amplitude modulation.

During MALA field-level inference on out-of-distribution (OoD) mock data, the posterior of $\theta_{\text{add}}$ systematically shifts negative for hydrodynamical (IllustrisTNG) maps (reflecting baryonic power suppression) and positive for source-redshift shifts of $\Delta z_s \approx 0.05\text{--}0.07$ (reflecting enhanced lensing efficiency).

Marginalizing over these latent degrees of freedom consistently reduces the OoD power-spectrum discrepancy metric $\mathcal{D}^2$ across 30 paired realizations ($500 \le \ell \le 10^4$) and improves non-Gaussian peak-count reconstructions compared to the latent-free baseline.
ai.relevance_reason: Directly addresses machine-learning surrogates/generative models trained on finite simulation suites, field-level inference for weak lensing, and physics-informed corrections motivated by super-survey modes (separate-universe-like effects).
ai.summary: In field-level cosmological inference, deep generative models are trained on expensive simulations to map initial Gaussian random fields directly to complex, non-linear observables like weak-lensing convergence ($\kappa$) maps. Because training suites contain a finite number of simulations, these models often suffer from "variance shrinkage"—accurately learning the ensemble-average statistics while underestimating the realization-to-realization scatter caused by cosmic variance and super-survey modes. The authors address this without running additional simulations by modifying the velocity field of a Continuous Normalizing Flow (CNF, a model that evolves Gaussian noise into non-Gaussian maps via an ordinary differential equation) trained on 10,000 gravity-only $\kappa\text{TNG}$ maps. Guided by how super-survey density modes affect local growth and mean density, they add a 20-parameter physics-informed latent correction to the flow dynamics and fit it to match higher-order moments of the field distribution. When performing field-level Bayesian reconstruction on noisy weak-lensing maps, these learned latent variables act as effective, scale-dependent nuisance parameters that restore missing sample variance and absorb out-of-distribution systematic errors like unmodeled baryonic feedback and photometric redshift shifts.

papers.title: Targeting the future of spectroscopic galaxy surveys -- A cosmological study case with the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope
papers.authors: Constantin Payerne, Antoine Rocher, Aurélien Verdier, William d'Assignies, Behnood Bandi, Sofia Contarini, Matteo Ferro, Jean-Paul Kneib, Vincenzo Mainieri, Michele Moresco, Marco Palla, Maxime Rombach, Christophe Yèche, Furkan Akbaba, Hélène Courtois, Darko Donevski, Massimo Guidi, Valentin Ivanov, Konstantinos Migkas, Ivan Minchev, Ignacio del Moral-Castro, Olcay Plevne, Mojtaba Raouf, Laurence Tresse, the WST Collaboration
papers.abstract: The next generation of Stage-V spectroscopic surveys are designed to measure hundreds of millions of galaxy and quasar spectra, extending precision large-scale-structure cosmology to redshifts and volumes well beyond the reach of current Stage-IV facilities. Realising this potential requires revisiting the target selection strategies and designing them explicitly around the depth, multiplexing, and survey time of the new instruments, rather than a direct extrapolation of existing recipes. This work develops and characterises new strategies for the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST), a proposed 12-metre, highly multiplexed facility expected to operate in the 2040s. Using deep multi-band photometry, including COSMOS-field data from CLAUDS and HSC, we revisit low-redshift $z<1.6$ tracer selection of SDSS, BOSS/eBOSS, DESI and 4MOST-CRS -- Bright Galaxies, Luminous Red Galaxies, Emission Line Galaxies and quasars -- to photometric depth achievable in the WST era, and introduce a purely magnitude-limited sample (MagMax) exploiting three-dimensional colour-colour star-galaxy separation, and a set of Lyman-Break Galaxy dropout samples extending target selection to $z>2$. Using Fisher-matrix forecasts, we showcase the constraining power of a WST-like cosmological survey on BAO distance parameters $\alpha_\parallel$ and $\alpha_\perp$, the growth rate $f$, the evolving dark energy equation $w_0w_a$, the local-type primordial non-Gaussianity $f_{\rm NL}^{\rm loc}$, and the sum of the neutrino mass $\Sigma m_\nu$. The main outcome of this work is an optimisation framework that directly links instrumental capabilities and observing time to cosmological constraining power, providing a science-driven template applicable to the design of future generations of Stage-V spectroscopic surveys.

conclusions: With a 12-metre aperture and 30,000 low-resolution fibres, WST can probe targets $\Delta m \sim 1.24$ magnitudes fainter than DESI in the same exposure time, requiring only 15 minutes (versus 2 hours for DESI) to reach $\mathrm{SNR}=20$ for an $r=24.2$ Lyman-Break Galaxy.

At low redshift ($z < 1.6$), the purely magnitude-limited "MagMax" sample—which uses 3D colour-colour star-galaxy separation rather than complex, tracer-specific colour cuts—achieves stellar contamination levels and cosmological constraints ($f\sigma_8$, BAO distances $D_A$ and $H$, and $w_0$–$w_a$) comparable to combining traditional Bright Galaxy, LRG, and ELG selections.

Extending target selection to $z > 2$ via $u$-, $g$-, and $r$-dropout Lyman-Break Galaxies unlocks huge, more linear cosmic volumes to simultaneously test the growth of structure, inflation ($f_{\mathrm{NL}}^{\mathrm{loc}}$), and total neutrino mass ($\sum m_\nu$).

Jointly optimising high-redshift magnitude limits and survey duration reveals distinct scaling behaviours: constraints on $f_{\mathrm{NL}}^{\mathrm{loc}}$ saturate rapidly with observing time because the relevant large scales quickly become cosmic-variance limited, whereas $\sum m_\nu$ constraints continue to improve over several years of additional observation thanks to progressive shot-noise suppression on small scales.
ai.relevance_reason: Provides broad background on how future Stage-V spectroscopic surveys will constrain $w_0w_a$ dynamical dark energy and structure growth ($f\sigma_8$), though it focuses on photometric target selection and linear Fisher forecasts rather than non-linear simulations, emulators, or inhomogeneous cosmology.
ai.summary: Future "Stage-V" spectroscopic facilities aim to map hundreds of millions of galaxy redshifts out to $z \sim 5$, pushing well beyond current Stage-IV surveys like DESI and Euclid to test evolving dark energy, neutrino masses, and primordial non-Gaussianity. Rather than simply scaling up traditional colour-cut target recipes, the authors develop a science-driven target selection and survey optimisation framework for the proposed Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST), a 12-metre, 32,000-fibre facility planned for the 2040s. Using deep multi-band photometry in the COSMOS field and an exposure time calculator, they evaluate rescaled DESI-like tracers alongside a new purely magnitude-limited low-redshift sample ("MagMax" at $z < 1.6$) and high-redshift Lyman-Break Galaxy (LBG) dropout samples ($z > 2$, selected via the sharp UV flux drop from neutral hydrogen absorption). They then propagate these realistic target densities, biases, and spectroscopic efficiencies through Fisher-matrix forecasts to directly link instrument observing time and limiting magnitudes to precision on BAO, redshift-space distortions, $w_0w_a$, $f_{\mathrm{NL}}^{\mathrm{loc}}$, and $\sum m_\nu$.

papers.title: DBI Softens Stiff-Phase Gravitational-Wave Spectra
papers.authors: Samuel Sánchez López, Eemeli Tomberg, Juan C. Bueno Sánchez
papers.abstract: We investigate the effect of non-canonical kinetic terms on the present-day density spectrum of primordial gravitational waves (GWs), by considering the dynamics of a scalar field governed by the Dirac--Born--Infeld (DBI) action and a runaway potential. The field, responsible for a period of inflation, subsequently enters a kinetically dominated regime, where the DBI structure reduces the equation-of-state parameter relative to the canonical kination result $w=1$, thereby softening the blue tilt of the GW spectrum. Simultaneously, the energy density of the field redshifts at a slower rate, delaying radiation domination and prolonging the stiff phase. The interplay between these two effects can lead to a potentially observable GW signal that would otherwise remain beyond the reach of future experiments in the canonical case. We test our predictions by numerically solving the background and perturbations, from inflation until radiation domination, and find viable parameter space compatible with cosmic microwave background and Big Bang Nucleosynthesis constraints.

conclusions: In the kinetically dominated post-inflationary regime ($X \gg V$), the DBI kinetic structure yields an equation of state $w^{(\phi)} \simeq c_s = 1/\gamma < 1$, reducing the present-day GW spectral slope $\text{d}\ln\Omega_{\text{GW}}^0/\text{d}\ln f$ from unity (canonical kination) to values between $0$ and $1$ for $1/3 < w^{(\phi)} < 1$.

An exponential warp factor $f(\phi) = f_0 e^{\kappa\phi/m_{\text{P}}}$ with $\sqrt{6} < \kappa < \sqrt{12}$ produces a sustained stiff phase with an approximately constant equation of state $w^{(\phi)} = 3/(\kappa^2 - 3)$, where $\kappa$ controls the spectral tilt and $f_0$ controls the duration before radiation domination.

By combining a softer high-frequency tilt (which avoids violating BBN $N_{\text{eff}}$ bounds) with a slower scalar energy density dilution ($\rho_\phi \propto a^{-3(1+w)}$) that prolongs the stiff era, the DBI model renders the primordial GW background detectable by future observatories across $\sim 10$ orders of magnitude in $f_0$ while remaining consistent with Planck 2018 and BICEP/Keck CMB constraints.

An analytical extension to constant-roll DBI backgrounds with an evolving sound speed shows that a stiff phase with average equation of state $0.487 \le \bar{w} \le 0.523$ can be sustained for $5$ to $20$ e-folds.
ai.summary: In standard inflation, primordial gravitational waves (GWs) that re-enter the horizon during the radiation-dominated era produce a nearly flat present-day energy density spectrum, $\Omega_{\text{GW}}^0(f)$. However, if the Universe first undergoes a "kination" phase—where the inflaton rolls down a steep runaway potential and its kinetic energy dominates over its potential energy—the background equation of state stiffens to $w=1$, imparting a steep blue tilt to the high-frequency GW spectrum that often either violates Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) radiation bounds or falls outside detector reach. The authors study how this picture changes when the inflaton is governed by a string-inspired Dirac–Born–Infeld (DBI) action, whose relativistic square-root kinetic term acts like a cosmic speed limit that keeps the sound speed $c_s$ and equation of state in the range $1/3 < w \simeq c_s < 1$ during kinetic domination. By numerically evolving the background and linear perturbations from inflation through radiation domination for an exponential brane warp factor, they show that the DBI dynamics both soften the blue tilt of $\Omega_{\text{GW}}^0(f)$ and slow the dilution of the scalar field, prolonging the stiff phase. This interplay opens a wide window of parameter space where the primordial GW signal evades BBN bounds while remaining detectable by future GW observatories.

papers.title: Multiprobe strategies for Kinematic Lensing with the Roman Space Telescope High Latitude Wide Area Survey
papers.authors: Yu-Hsiu Huang, Jiachuan Xu, Tim Eifler, Elisabeth Krause, Spencer Everett, Fabian Hervas-Peters, Pranjal R. S., Eric Huff, Yan Xiang Lai
papers.abstract: In its latest design, the High Latitude Wide Area Survey (HLWAS) Medium Tier comprises overlapping photometric and spectroscopic data across 2,300 square degrees. This dataset enables Kinematic Lensing (KL), a Weak Lensing (WL) technique that exploits galaxy kinematics to control for shape noise, the dominant statistical limitation of traditional WL. We present several simulated analyses quantifying the expected cosmological science return of a Roman KL analysis with the latest design of the HLWAS: We explore KL prospects with early Roman data from the Deep Tier fields and from the early Medium Tier fields; we demonstrate the impact of different roll-angle choices on the KL performance; we benchmark KL against traditional WL; we introduce a KL-based multiprobe analysis that jointly models KL, galaxy clustering, and galaxy-galaxy lensing. In these analyses, we consider systematics, including photometric uncertainties, shear calibration bias, galaxy bias, and baryonic feedback. Our results show that KL alone achieves a dark energy figure of merit (FoM) of 22.54, which is more than a factor of two improvement over a corresponding WL analysis. The KL multiprobe approach improves the full-survey FoM to 34.58, even assuming conservative scale cuts in the clustering and galaxy-galaxy lensing. For the HLWAS roll-angle strategy, we find that the current plan of 4 passes with rotations of approximately 0, 10, 170, 180 degrees are near optimal for KL.

conclusions: Kinematic lensing (KL) alone in the $2,300\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ Roman HLWAS Medium Tier achieves a $w_0w_a$ dark energy Figure of Merit (FoM) of $22.54$, more than doubling the constraining power of traditional photometric weak lensing in the same footprint, with $700\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ of Year 1 KL data already matching the 5-year WL forecast.

Extending KL to a multiprobe $3\times 2\mathrm{pt}$ analysis—using the spectroscopic KL galaxies ($n_{\mathrm{gal}} = 3.9\,\mathrm{arcmin}^{-2}$) as both sources and lenses—boosts the full-survey dark energy FoM to $34.58$ even under conservative scale cuts, though narrow tomographic bins require non-Limber clustering calculations to avoid parameter bias.

Mock observations of broadband images and 2D grism spectra confirm that Roman's planned 4-pass roll-angle strategy ($\approx 0^\circ, 10^\circ, 170^\circ, 180^\circ$) is near-optimal for breaking the degeneracy between shear and intrinsic galaxy inclination/position angle.

Because KL suppresses shape noise by an order of magnitude, small-scale measurements become signal-dominated rather than shot-noise-limited, making baryonic feedback modeling the primary systematic bottleneck for extracting further cosmological information.
ai.relevance_reason: Provides useful background on weak lensing, $3\times 2\mathrm{pt}$ multiprobe methodology, and dynamical dark energy ($w_0w_a$) forecasts for a Stage-IV survey, though it focuses on Roman observational strategies rather than Euclid, beyond-$\Lambda$CDM simulations, or inhomogeneous cosmology.
ai.summary: Traditional weak lensing (WL) is statistically limited by 'shape noise'—because we do not know a galaxy's true unlensed shape, we must average over millions of galaxies to detect the tiny coherent distortions caused by gravitational lensing. Kinematic Lensing (KL) overcomes this bottleneck for disk galaxies by combining broadband imaging with spectroscopy: measuring a galaxy's rotation velocity via the Tully–Fisher relation and mapping its 2D velocity field breaks the degeneracy between intrinsic inclination and lensing shear, drastically reducing shape noise and eliminating key WL systematics like photometric redshift errors and intrinsic alignments. In this paper, the authors use the `CosmoLike` framework and pixel-level `kl-tools` mock observations to forecast the cosmological performance of KL for the updated design of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's High Latitude Wide Area Survey (HLWAS) Medium Tier, which provides overlapping imaging and slitless grism spectroscopy across $2,300\,\mathrm{deg}^2$. They evaluate how telescope roll-angle separations affect 2D grism spectra decontamination and introduce a spectroscopic 'KL-$3\times 2\mathrm{pt}$' multiprobe analysis that combines KL cosmic shear, galaxy-galaxy lensing, and galaxy clustering while accounting for baryonic feedback via principal components trained on hydrodynamical simulations.

papers.title: Baryonic feedback and intrinsic alignments in profile: a frequentist view of DES Y3 cosmic shear
papers.authors: Anoma Ganguly, Elisabeth Krause, Tanvi Karwal, Vivian Miranda
papers.abstract: Current cosmic shear surveys primarily constrain $S_8$ and $\Omega_\mathrm{m}$, while most other model parameters remain dominated by priors. Consequently, marginal posteriors are vulnerable to prior-volume effects, particularly through degeneracies among $S_8$, baryonic feedback, and intrinsic alignment (IA) model parameters. To isolate data-driven constraints from prior volume effects, we compare profile likelihoods with Bayesian posteriors for DES Y3 cosmic shear under the DES Y3+KiDS-1000 Hybrid model. For cosmic shear alone, the profile global best fit and the marginal posterior mean agree in $S_8$, but the profile likelihood reveals a strong degeneracy between feedback strength and $S_8$, leaving the upper $1\sigma$ limit on $S_8$ determined by the assumed feedback range. External CMB information on parameters other than $\Omega_\mathrm{m}$ and $S_8$ breaks this degeneracy, suppressing prior-volume effects and reconciling the profiles with the posteriors. With CMB data included, small-scale cosmic shear data prefers moderate baryonic feedback strengths consistent with hydrodynamical simulations calibrated to observed gas fractions. Furthermore, additional unconstrained parameters in the tidal alignment and tidal torquing (TATT) model result in weaker constraints, shifting and broadening the $S_8$ profile relative to the nonlinear linear alignment (NLA) model. Adding DES Y3 shear ratios mitigates this degeneracy, bringing profile likelihood and marginal posteriors into close agreement.

conclusions: For DES Y3 cosmic shear alone, the $S_8$ profile likelihood is noticeably broader than the Bayesian marginal posterior because unconstrained cosmological and nuisance parameters are driven to the edges of their allowed ranges, where negligible prior volume artificially shrinks the Bayesian posterior.

Cosmic-shear-only constraints on the upper $1\sigma$ limit of $S_8$ are limited by a strong degeneracy with the baryonic feedback parameter $\log_{10}(T_{\mathrm{AGN}}/\mathrm{K})$, where stronger small-scale power suppression compensates for higher clustering amplitudes.

Adding CMB information (specifically on $\omega_{\mathrm{b}}$, $n_{\mathrm{s}}$, and $h$) breaks the shape degeneracies of the matter power spectrum, bringing the profile likelihood and Bayesian posterior into close agreement and yielding $S_8$ consistent with Planck within $1.0\sigma$ (profile) and $1.3\sigma$ (posterior), while preferring moderate baryonic feedback matching hydrodynamical simulations.

Replacing the 2-parameter NLA intrinsic alignment model with the 5-parameter TATT model shifts and broadens the $S_8$ profile due to newly opened degenerate directions, though incorporating DES Y3 shear-ratio data successfully breaks these degeneracies and reconciles the frequentist and Bayesian constraints.
ai.relevance_reason: Directly addresses the $S_8$ tension, weak lensing non-linear modelling (baryonic feedback and intrinsic alignments), and emulator-accelerated cosmological inference, which are core medium-relevance topics for your Euclid work.
ai.summary: Cosmic shear (the coherent distortion of background galaxy shapes by foreground weak gravitational lensing) primarily constrains the matter clustering parameter $S_8$ and matter density $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$, leaving many astrophysical nuisance parameters poorly constrained. In standard Bayesian analyses, integrating (marginalizing) over these weakly constrained parameters—such as baryonic feedback (gas heating by active galactic nuclei, parameterized by $T_{\mathrm{AGN}}$, which suppresses small-scale structure) and intrinsic alignments (IA, the physical alignment of galaxy shapes with local tidal fields, modeled via the simpler NLA or extended TATT frameworks)—can induce "prior-volume effects" that shift or artificially tighten posterior constraints. To isolate purely data-driven constraints from prior effects, the authors construct a fast frequentist profile likelihood pipeline (which maximizes rather than integrates the likelihood at each parameter value) using a neural-network power spectrum emulator (`CosmoPower` for `HMCode2020`) and the CMA-ES optimizer, applying it to the KiDS-excised DES Y3 cosmic shear dataset. This matters because it reveals how much of the apparent $S_8$ constraint and its tension with the CMB in cosmic-shear-only analyses is genuinely driven by lensing data versus prior boundaries on feedback and IA parameters.

papers.title: Toward the one- and two-loop EFTofLSS for Simons Observatory CMB lensing
papers.authors: Evan Saraivanov, Henrique Rubira, Vivian Miranda
papers.abstract: Cosmic microwave background (CMB) lensing observations are becoming sensitive to non-linear structure formation and baryonic feedback scenarios. The effective field theory of large-scale structure (EFTofLSS) provides a systematic description of matter clustering in the mildly non-linear regime, accounting for baryonic effects through counterterms and offering a consistent framework for cross-correlations with other observables. We perform a Fisher forecast for the joint Simons Observatory temperature, polarization, and CMB lensing likelihood using noiseless data vectors with different baryonic feedback scenarios, modelling non-linear structure formation using the one- and two-loop EFTofLSS. We find that, with a single additional parameter, obtained through a principal-component analysis of the EFTofLSS counterterms, both the one- and two-loop EFTofLSS provide a good fit across the baryonic feedback scenarios considered. This parameter is closely aligned with the effective AGN heating temperature $T_{\rm AGN}$. Both loop orders reduce cosmological parameter biases, with only a small loss in marginalized precision at fixed scale cuts. We find that the one-loop EFTofLSS yields unbiased estimates over a range of scales similar to the dark-matter-only model, while the two-loop EFTofLSS extends this range to smaller scales and accommodates different feedback scenarios more robustly. When each model is evaluated at the smallest scales for which its cosmological parameter estimates remain unbiased, the two-loop EFTofLSS yields stronger constraints than the dark-matter-only model.

conclusions: Despite parameterizing the redshift evolution of the EFTofLSS counterterms up to $z=50$ with 32 spline knots per coefficient (yielding up to 160 parameters at two-loop), PCA compression shows that varying just a single principal component is enough to keep 1D cosmological parameter biases below $\sim 0.2\sigma$ across all tested baryonic feedback models, with this mode acting primarily as an effective proxy for the AGN heating temperature $T_{\rm AGN}$.

Two-loop EFTofLSS maintains a good fit ($\Delta\chi^2 < 0.2$) up to $k_{\rm UV,0} \approx 0.6\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$, tripling the wavenumber reach of one-loop EFTofLSS ($k_{\rm UV,0} \approx 0.2\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$).

At a fixed scale cut, marginalizing over the leading EFTofLSS principal component reduces the overall cosmological Figure of Merit (FoM) by $\sim 30\%$ (only a few percent loss per 1D parameter) compared to a dark-matter-only HMCode baseline.

When each model is evaluated at the smallest scales where it remains unbiased, two-loop EFTofLSS outperforms the dark-matter-only model's FoM by a few percent under weak baryonic feedback and by up to $40\%$ under strong feedback, whereas one-loop EFTofLSS still suffers a $\sim 20\%$ FoM loss.
ai.relevance_reason: Directly addresses perturbation theory for LSS (one- and two-loop EFTofLSS with neural-network IR-resummed emulators), non-linear power spectrum modelling, and $w_0w_a$CDM forecasts using DESI BAO + DES-Y5 priors.
ai.summary: As CMB experiments like the Simons Observatory (SO) map the sky with higher precision, gravitational lensing of CMB photons by intervening matter becomes sensitive to small-scale non-linear clustering and baryonic feedback (such as active galactic nuclei, or AGN, heating and expelling gas from halos). If unmodelled, these poorly understood small-scale physics bias cosmological parameter inference, especially because line-of-sight lensing projections mix high-$k$ modes into larger angular scales. The authors tackle this by applying one- and two-loop Effective Field Theory of Large-Scale Structure (EFTofLSS)—which systematically absorbs unresolved small-scale and baryonic physics into perturbative counterterms—to a joint Fisher forecast of SO lensed CMB temperature/polarization and CMB lensing power spectra in a $w_0w_a$CDM cosmology. Using neural network emulators for the IR-resummed loop integrals, cubic splines for the counterterms' redshift evolution up to $z=50$, and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) alongside strict UV-sensitivity scale cuts, they show that two-loop EFTofLSS can robustly marginalize over diverse hydrodynamical feedback scenarios with minimal nuisance parameters while extracting more small-scale cosmological information than standard dark-matter-only halo models.

papers.title: Detection of the Galaxy--Galaxy--Temperature Skewed Bispectrum
papers.authors: I. J. Keja, D. Karagiannis, W. R. Coulton, P. D. Meerburg
papers.abstract: We present the first measurement of the galaxy--galaxy--temperature skewed bispectrum, obtained by cross-correlating the squared, filtered unWISE galaxy overdensity with \textit{Planck} maps at 100, 143, 217, and 353~GHz. The signal is detected with high significance in all four channels. Its frequency dependence reveals contributions from hot gas through the thermal Sunyaev--Zel'dovich (tSZ) effect and from dust through the cosmic infrared background (CIB). With the galaxy occupation fixed, our halo-model fits favor higher integrated pressure and peak star-formation efficiency for the galaxy--temperature cross-spectra than for the skewed bispectrum. Comparisons with component-separated tSZ and CIB maps from the same \textit{Planck} observations indicate that this mismatch is not confined to the frequency-map fits. This difference motivates testing more flexible descriptions of gas pressure, CIB emission, and galaxy occupation. In particular, it could point to a mass dependence of the gas-pressure profile that our model does not fully capture. By giving greater weight to massive halos that host many galaxy pairs, the skewed bispectrum provides a complementary test of these descriptions, using information beyond two-point statistics at a comparable computational cost.

conclusions: First detection of the galaxy–galaxy–temperature skewed bispectrum ($C_L^{g^2 T_\nu}$) across four *Planck* HFI frequency channels (100–353 GHz), achieving a joint signal-to-noise ratio of $\text{S/N} = 110$ (detection significance $>13\sigma$ in every individual channel) and cleanly separating the negative tSZ decrement at 100/143 GHz from positive CIB dust emission at 217/353 GHz.

Fitting a halo model with fixed galaxy occupation yields a dimensionless integrated cluster gas pressure within $5R_{500}$ of $\log_{10} Y_{5R_{500}} = 0.144^{+0.048}_{-0.047}$ ($\sim 11\%$ precision) for the skewed bispectrum, whereas the standard two-point cross-spectrum ($gT$) yields $\log_{10} Y_{5R_{500}} = 0.580^{+0.029}_{-0.032}$ ($\sim 7\%$ precision).

The two-point cross-spectrum prefers $2.7\times$ higher integrated gas pressure and $1.9\times$ higher peak star-formation efficiency than the skewed bispectrum; mapped onto a fixed *Planck* reference pressure profile, this corresponds to an effective hydrostatic mass bias of $B \approx 2.7$ for $g^2 T$ versus $B \approx 1.5$ for $gT$.

Cross-checks with component-separated *Planck* Compton-$y$ and CIB maps confirm that this tension is not an artifact of frequency separation, pointing instead to unmodeled mass dependence in cluster gas-pressure profiles (baryonic feedback), inaccuracies in how the HOD places galaxy pairs in massive halos, or neglected non-Gaussian covariance terms.
ai.relevance_reason: Provides useful background on fast higher-order LSS summary statistics (skew-spectra) and halo-model descriptions of baryonic gas pressure on nonlinear scales, though it focuses on astrophysical tSZ/CIB cross-correlations rather than beyond-$\Lambda$CDM simulations or emulators.
ai.summary: When cosmic microwave background (CMB) photons travel through large-scale structure, they interact with hot ionized gas in galaxy clusters via the thermal Sunyaev–Zel'dovich (tSZ) effect and are supplemented by thermal dust emission from star-forming galaxies known as the cosmic infrared background (CIB). While two-point cross-correlations between galaxy positions and microwave temperature maps ($gT$) weight host dark matter halos by their mean galaxy count, three-point correlations ($ggT$) weight halos by their number of galaxy pairs—making them much more sensitive to massive, galaxy-rich clusters. To extract this higher-order information without the heavy computational cost of evaluating all bispectrum triangles, the authors filter and square the projected unWISE Blue galaxy overdensity field ($\bar{z} \simeq 0.6$) and cross-correlate it with *Planck* temperature maps at 100, 143, 217, and 353 GHz to measure the "skewed bispectrum" ($g^2 T$). Fitting a halo model with a fixed galaxy halo occupation distribution (HOD), they find that the skewed bispectrum prefers significantly lower integrated gas pressure and star-formation efficiency than the standard $gT$ cross-spectrum. This mismatch demonstrates that combining two- and three-point galaxy–CMB statistics provides a sharp, computationally cheap test of how baryonic gas, dust, and satellite galaxies populate massive halos across different mass scales.

papers.title: Mercury (Hg): a relativistic $N$-body simulation for Horndeski gravity
papers.authors: Ahmad Nouri-Zonoz, Farbod Hassani, Julian Adamek, Emilio Bellini, Martin Kunz
papers.abstract: We present Mercury, a relativistic $N$-body code for cosmological simulations in the $\alpha$-basis formulation of Horndeski gravity. Mercury extends a particle-mesh scheme by incorporating the dynamics of the additional scalar degree of freedom and the corresponding modified Einstein equations, expressed in terms of the time-dependent functions $\alpha_{\rm K}, \alpha_{\rm B}, \alpha_{\rm M}, \alpha_{\rm T}$ and the effective Planck mass $M_*^2$. This generalises our previous implementation of Horndeski subclass models, namely $k$-essence and kinetic gravity braiding (KGB), to the general linear Horndeski $\alpha$-basis. The code evolves the additional scalar degree of freedom and its effective stress--energy tensor alongside the nonlinear matter and metric fields, so that nonlinear structure formation sources the scalar-field evolution and feeds back on the gravitational potentials. Through its interface with hi_class, Mercury supports both phenomenological $\alpha$-function parametrisations and covariant Horndeski theories; we demonstrate the latter using nKGB, the Cubic Galileon, and Brans--Dicke models. We validate the implementation against hi_class in the linear regime and recover the expected nonlinear $k$-essence and KGB limits. For the luminal Horndeski models considered here, we show how a running effective Planck mass generates gravitational slip through the scalar anisotropic stress and modifies the friction terms governing the vector and tensor metric perturbations. The evolution of $M_*^2$ also modifies the normalisation and scale dependence of the effective dark-energy density contrast, leaving a corresponding imprint on its power spectrum. The present framework provides an intermediate step towards nonlinear Horndeski simulations, in which nonlinear scalar self-interactions and screening effects can be incorporated consistently within the same relativistic framework.

conclusions: Mercury successfully bridges the linear Horndeski solver `hi_class` with `gevolution` (including GPU acceleration via `gevolution 2.0`), supporting both phenomenological EFT $\alpha$-function parametrisations and full covariant models (validated on Brans–Dicke, Cubic Galileon, and nKGB).

A non-zero Planck-mass run rate ($\alpha_{\rm M} \neq 0$, meaning an evolving effective gravitational strength $M_*^2$) directly generates gravitational slip ($\Phi \neq \Psi$) via scalar anisotropic stress, alters the friction/damping terms for vector and tensor metric perturbations, and changes both the normalisation and scale dependence of the dark-energy density power spectrum.

Because the scalar field itself is evolved using linear perturbation equations (with nonlinearities arising only from its coupling to the nonlinear matter and metric fields), this release captures backreaction onto the metric potentials without yet modelling nonlinear scalar self-interactions or Vainshtein/chameleon screening.

Resolution convergence tests up to $3072^3$ particles/grid cells in a $4000\,h^{-1}\text{Mpc}$ box show that individual matter and dark-energy power spectra converge to within $2\%$ up to $k \simeq 0.29\,h\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}$ and $0.36\,h\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}$ respectively, while power spectrum ratios between different models cancel grid effects and remain accurate to within $\sim 1\text{--}2\%$ to much smaller scales.
ai.relevance_reason: This paper presents a relativistic N-body simulation code for modified gravity (Horndeski/Brans–Dicke/Galileon) and includes a researcher from your own institute (Farbod Hassani at ITA Oslo), hitting both your core topics of beyond-ΛCDM N-body simulations and relativistic cosmological modelling.
ai.summary: Horndeski gravity is the most general scalar-tensor framework for dark energy and modified gravity that avoids unstable higher-derivative ghosts, and on linear scales its behaviour is neatly summarised by the effective Planck mass $M_*^2$ and four time-dependent Effective Field Theory (EFT) functions: kineticity ($\alpha_{\rm K}$), kinetic braiding ($\alpha_{\rm B}$), Planck-mass run rate ($\alpha_{\rm M}$), and tensor speed excess ($\alpha_{\rm T}$). To push tests of these theories into the nonlinear regime of structure formation while keeping full relativistic effects, the authors introduce **Mercury**, an extension of the relativistic particle-mesh $N$-body code `gevolution` that interfaces directly with the Einstein–Boltzmann solver `hi_class`. Mercury evolves matter and weak-field metric perturbations (scalar, vector, and tensor modes in the Poisson gauge) nonlinearly alongside the Horndeski scalar field, which is governed by its linear $\alpha$-basis perturbation equations but dynamically sourced by the nonlinear matter and metric fields. This provides a unified, GPU-accelerated relativistic simulation pipeline for both phenomenological $\alpha$-parametrisations and covariant theories like Brans–Dicke and Cubic Galileon, serving as a crucial stepping stone toward full nonlinear scalar screening in relativistic $N$-body simulations.

papers.title: A Composite Rest-Frame UV Spectrum of Galaxies at $5.7 < z < 6.9$: Ionization, Outflows, and Implications for Intergalactic Metal Enrichment
papers.authors: David DePalma, Robert A. Simcoe, Anna-Christina Eilers, Rongmon Bordoloi, Daichi Kashino, Gauri Kotiwale, Jorryt Matthee
papers.abstract: We present a stacked JWST/NIRSpec spectrum of 104 galaxies at $\lambda_{\rm rest}=1200\unicode{x2013}2000\;\mathrm{\mathring{A}}$ to study nebular emission and absorption from the interstellar medium (ISM) and stellar winds. The sample is drawn from known [O III] emitters with mean redshift $z=6.50$, absolute UV magnitude $M_\mathrm{UV}=-20.7$, and stellar mass $M_{\star}=10^{8.93}\;\mathrm{M_\odot}$. The stacked continuum closely resembles lower-redshift Lyman Break Galaxy composites, with a few notable differences. Ly$\;\alpha$ has comparable strength and is redshifted relative to the [O III] systemic frame, consistent with production in gaseous outflows. High-ionization emission lines including O III], C III], and He II are slightly stronger than in lower-redshift stacks but exhibit narrow widths, disfavoring ionization from a broad-line AGN. Emission-line ratios slightly favor ionization by a hard stellar continuum, though a contribution from a narrow-line nuclear source cannot be strictly excluded. Numerous strong absorption lines at both high and low ionization are blueshifted by $\sim200\;\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, again indicating outflows driven by stellar winds or entrained metal-enriched ISM. A simple model suggests that at $z\sim6.5$ most star-forming galaxies are too young for winds at these velocities to propagate beyond $\sim3\unicode{x2013}9$ proper kpc, implying that the observed [O III] emitter population alone cannot explain the frequency of heavy-element absorbers seen in quasar spectra. In this picture, early enrichment of the intergalactic medium likely arises from undetected low-mass galaxies ($M_\star\sim10^5\unicode{x2013}10^6\;\mathrm{M_\odot}$) clustered around the more massive systems detected in JWST/NIRCam WFSS surveys.

conclusions: The $z \sim 6.5$ composite rest-UV spectrum is remarkably similar to $z \sim 3$ Lyman-break galaxy stacks in both continuum shape and absorption profiles, but exhibits stronger, narrow high-ionization emission lines ($\text{O III]}$, $\text{C III]}$, and $\text{He II}$), pointing to harder ionizing radiation from young, hot stars rather than broad-line AGN.

Interstellar absorption lines across both low- and high-ionization species are systematically blueshifted by $\sim 170\text{--}200\;\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ relative to the systemic $[\text{O III}]$ rest frame (while $\text{Ly}\alpha$ is redshifted by $\sim 250\;\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$), providing clear evidence for widespread galactic outflows during the late reionization era.

Kinematic modeling using a typical star-formation duration of $t_{20} \sim 38\;\mathrm{Myr}$ shows that $200\;\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ winds can only reach maximum radii of $R_{\rm max} \sim 3\text{--}9$ proper kpc, meaning these wind bubbles account for $< 1\%$ of the heavy-element absorber incidence ($dN/dX$) observed in background quasar spectra.

Because observable $[\text{O III}]$-emitting galaxies cannot enrich large enough volumes in the available cosmic time, the bulk of early intergalactic metal enrichment must instead come from a much more numerous population of faint, undetected dwarf galaxies ($M_\star \sim 10^5\text{--}10^6\;M_\odot$) clustered around the brighter JWST-detected systems.
ai.summary: During the epoch of reionization ($z \gtrsim 6$), distant quasar spectra already show absorption from heavy elements ("metals") in the intergalactic medium (IGM), raising the question of how early galaxies managed to expel enriched gas across cosmic distances in such a short amount of cosmic time. To investigate the galactic winds driving this enrichment, the authors stacked rest-frame ultraviolet JWST/NIRSpec spectra of 104 star-forming galaxies at $5.7 < z < 6.9$ (mean $z = 6.50$ and stellar mass $M_\star \approx 10^{8.9}\;M_\odot$) from the MASQUERADE survey, using rest-frame optical $[\text{O III}]$ emission lines to anchor the exact systemic redshift of each galaxy. By fitting the composite emission and absorption line profiles and coupling the measured outflow speeds with a simple kinematic wind-propagation model, they tested whether the observed galaxy population can physically pollute the surrounding IGM fast enough. They found that while these galaxies do host active outflows, their winds have not had enough time to travel far from their host halos, implying that the metals seen in quasar spectra must instead originate from much fainter, unseen dwarf galaxies clustered nearby.

papers.title: On the Role of Gravity in Supercooled Phase Transitions
papers.authors: Filippo Cutrona, Alberto Salvio
papers.abstract: Theories with radiative mass generation and radiative symmetry breaking (RSB) lead to first-order phase transitions (FOPTs) and the production of gravitational waves (GWs) as well as primordial black holes if supercooling lasts long enough. Here we investigate the role of gravity in supercooled FOPTs that occur in the RSB scenario. We use a model-independent approach that is valid when a quantity (which we explicitly determine and is computable once the model is specified) is small enough. Eventually, the curvature of spacetime becomes relevant if the FOPT does not complete in the case in which gravity is ignored.
